planting.note: Root offsets or stem cuttings in spring in lean, fast-draining succulent mix; this species tolerates cooler nights better than many of its relatives, since it grows naturally in shaded canyon rock crevices at higher elevation along the Arizona-Sonora borderlands.

directions: Grow in lean, fast-draining succulent mix in bright, filtered light or partial shade, mimicking the sheltered canyon rock crevices where this species grows wild, and let the soil dry out between waterings. Loose rosettes of thick, powdery pale gray-green to lavender-blue leaves cluster on short stems, slowly forming small mounded colonies as offsets develop around the base. Clusters of small white flowers with maroon speckling rise on slender stalks above the foliage in late winter to spring. It handles cooler nights better than many warmth-loving relatives, so it suits a sheltered rock garden in milder climates as well as container culture elsewhere.

planting.note: Root offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix; give this larger-growing species more room to spread than smaller graptopetalums since mature rosettes can reach several inches across.

directions: Plant in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in full sun to bright light, watering deeply and then allowing the soil to dry completely before the next watering. This is one of the larger species in its genus, forming substantial rosettes of thick, broad, gray-green leaves often flushed with a reddish-bronze tint and a faint powdery coating along the margins. Loose clusters of star-shaped white to pale yellow flowers appear on arching stalks in late winter or spring, followed by the slow development of basal offsets that can be separated once rooted. Native to rocky slopes in Sonora and Sinaloa, Mexico, it makes a striking specimen in a mixed succulent bed or large container.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Root offsets or stem cuttings in spring in lean, gritty succulent mix; this Baja California native is well suited to dry, low-humidity climates and resents consistently damp soil.

directions: Grow in lean, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light, watering only once the soil has dried out completely to prevent rot. Compact rosettes of pale blue-green to grayish leaves cluster on short stems and spread by offsets, gradually forming a low, tidy mat over time. Small white to cream flowers appear on short stalks above the foliage, typically in late winter into spring. Native to arid rocky habitats in Baja California Sur, Mexico, it is well adapted to low-humidity, low-water container culture and rock gardens in frost-free climates.

planting.note: Root offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix; strong light intensifies the pink leaf-margin color that gives this species much of its appeal.

directions: Grow in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in full sun to bright light, letting the soil dry out completely between waterings. Compact, tightly packed rosettes of powdery blue-gray leaves are edged in pink to coral-red, a color that deepens with stronger light and cooler nights, and the species offsets readily to form dense clusters over time. Coral-pink, bell-shaped flowers rise on arching stalks above the foliage in spring, attracting pollinators. Native to the state of Chihuahua in northern Mexico, it is a popular, easy-care rosette succulent for containers, rock gardens, and mixed succulent plantings in frost-free climates.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; crowding the stacked leaves too close to glass or reflective surfaces can scorch them in intense summer sun.

directions: Grow in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix in bright light to full sun, watering only once the soil has dried out completely. Thick, grayish-green, wart-covered leaves are stacked tightly in opposite pairs up a stout, upright stem, giving the plant a sculptural, almost geometric appearance prized by collectors. Small white to pale pink flowers cluster near the stem tip in summer, and offsets occasionally form at the base of older plants. Native to arid regions of South Africa and Namibia, it is slow-growing and well suited to a dedicated collector's pot rather than a mixed planting, since its unusual form is best appreciated on its own.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Divide offsets in spring and pot into lean, fast-draining succulent mix; mature rosettes are typically short-lived and decline after flowering, so keeping young offsets coming along ensures the planting persists.

directions: Grow in lean, fast-draining succulent mix in full sun to bright light, watering sparingly and allowing the soil to dry out fully between waterings. Pairs of thick, rounded gray-green leaves stack flat atop one another to form a tight, squat column, an unusual growth habit that makes this one of the more architectural dwarf crassulas. A single rosette typically flowers once, sending up a dense spike of small star-shaped flowers before that particular growth point declines, but offsets produced at the base carry the colony forward. Native to winter-rainfall regions of South Africa, it is best grown in a shallow collector's pot with other small, slow-growing succulents rather than in a crowded mixed planting.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Root offsets or stem sections in spring in lean, fast-draining succulent mix; this species is a parent of the popular hybrid Buddha's Temple and shares its preference for bright light without harsh midday scorch.

directions: Grow in lean, fast-draining succulent mix in bright light to gentle morning sun, letting the soil dry out completely between waterings. Narrow, triangular gray-green leaves are packed tightly in opposite pairs along an upright stem with almost no visible gaps, creating a distinctive segmented, cylindrical form that resembles a rattlesnake's tail or a zipper pull. Tiny white flowers are nearly hidden within the leaf tips near the stem apex, blooming in summer. Native to rocky outcrops in South Africa's Western Cape, it is slow-growing and best displayed alone in a narrow collector's pot where its unusual stacked form can be fully appreciated.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Root offsets in spring in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; keep water off the leaf surface since the raised white texture can trap moisture and invite rot if it stays wet.

directions: Grow in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light, watering from below when possible and letting the soil dry out completely between waterings. Thick, rounded gray-green leaves are densely covered in raised, wart-like white papillae that give the foliage a crusty, footprint-like texture unlike any other common crassula. Small white to pale pink flowers appear in compact clusters above the rosette in winter to early spring. Native to the Western Cape of South Africa, it offsets slowly to form small clumps and is best grown in a shallow pot where its unusual leaf texture is easy to see up close.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Root stem-tip cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix; the scrambling stems benefit from a hanging basket or a trellis to climb, since they do not stay upright on their own for long.

directions: Grow in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix in bright light to partial sun, letting the mix dry out between waterings. Scalloped-edged, triangular green leaves with faint reddish margins are carried in opposite pairs along slender, scrambling stems that trail from a container or climb low supports if given the chance. Clusters of small white, faintly fragrant, star-shaped flowers appear mostly in winter on mature growth. It roots easily wherever a stem touches soil, making it simple to propagate and a good choice for a hanging basket or as a trailing accent spilling over the edge of a mixed succulent planter.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Root stem or leaf cuttings in spring in fast-draining succulent mix; this species flowers more reliably than many crassulas and rewards a dry winter rest with a showier bloom in fall.

directions: Grow in fast-draining succulent mix in full sun to bright light, watering thoroughly and then allowing the soil to dry out completely before watering again. Glossy, dark green, pointed leaves are dotted along the margins with small raised white spots and come to a slender tip, a detail that gives the species its descriptive name. In fall, mature plants produce abundant clusters of small, fragrant, star-shaped white flowers that can nearly cover the foliage, making it one of the more floriferous crassulas in cultivation. It forms a shrubby, long-lived clump over time and is easily propagated from stem or leaf cuttings allowed to callus before rooting.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring in lean, fast-draining succulent mix; the hairy leaf surface holds moisture longer than smooth-leaved crassulas, so err toward underwatering rather than overwatering.

directions: Grow in lean, fast-draining succulent mix in full sun to bright light, letting the soil dry out fully between waterings since the fuzzy leaf surface holds humidity longer than smooth-leaved relatives. Plump, cylindrical, pale green leaves are covered in soft white bristly hairs and packed in congested, upright columns, a texture that recalls a hairy ice plant and gives the species its name. Small white flowers appear in compact clusters near the stem tips, typically in summer. Native to the winter-rainfall regions of South Africa, it is slow-growing and best suited to a dedicated collector's pot with sharp drainage rather than a crowded mixed planting.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference
